title: Tensor–Hom form of the exchange
statement:
Let $f:X\to Y$ be a separated finite-type morphism of finite-type
$k$-schemes, with $f^!=Rf^!$ the constructible exceptional adjoint of
[sk-def-sf-operations] (vi) (no admissibility datum is assumed), and let
$M\in\Dctf(X,\Lambda)$ and $N\in\Dctf(Y,\Lambda)$. Then there is a canonical isomorphism

$$
Rf_*\RHom_X(M,f^!N)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\RHom_Y(Rf_!M,N),
$$

in the ambient category $D^+(Y,\Lambda)$, natural in $M$ and $N$ and
compatible with finite reduction, scalar extension and shifts.

proof.text:
First establish the actual tensor–Hom bijection, rather than take it from a definition of the operations. On any of the small ringed sites $\mathcal C$ in the datum, write $H(P,Q)=R\mathcal Hom(P,Q)$. The two cited statements give, naturally in $L,P,Q$,
$$\operatorname{Hom}(L,H(P,Q))
\cong H^0(\mathcal C,H(L,H(P,Q)))
\cong H^0(\mathcal C,H(L\otimes^L P,Q))
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L\otimes^L P,Q).$$
The outer bijections are the global-sections identification and the middle one is internal-Hom currying. Interchanging the tensor factors gives the convention $P\otimes^L L$ used below. These bijections are the adjunction with evaluation as counit. At finite coefficients this is the ambient, uncompleted tensor–Hom adjunction; no site-perfectness assumption is made.

proof.text:
At $R=\mathcal O_E$, let $P,L,Q$ be integral bounded constructible objects on a scheme $W$, and put $T=P\otimes^L_{\widehat R_W}L$, using the ordinary ambient tensor only in this paragraph. The completed tensor in the datum is
$$P\widehat\otimes^L_R L=R\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Res}_n(P_n\otimes^L_{A_n}L_n).$$
Its tower is the quotient tower of $T$: on K-flat representatives, the balancing isomorphism is $(p\otimes a)\otimes(l\otimes b)\mapsto(p\otimes l)\otimes ab$, with inverse $(p\otimes l)\otimes a\mapsto(p\otimes1)\otimes(l\otimes a)$. It commutes with differentials and quotient transitions. The constant/completed-coefficient comparison identifies this quotient limit, with its unit, with the Koszul completion of $T$ over $\widehat R_W$. It also identifies the local and Koszul completeness conditions. The integral definition makes $Q$ isomorphic to a quotient limit of its reductions; that limit is a completion by the same comparison, hence $Q$ satisfies the local completeness condition needed by the reflector. Apply the reflector's mapping property, then step 1:
$$\operatorname{Hom}(P\widehat\otimes^L_R L,Q)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(P\otimes^L_{\widehat R_W}L,Q)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L,H(P,Q)).$$
Every arrow is natural and induced by the completion unit or evaluation. This proves the needed completed tensor–Hom adjunction by composing existing statements; it does not identify the two tensor objects. The Noetherian coefficient ring is $R$, the ideal is $(\varpi_E)$, and the site is small, exactly as required by the cited completion comparison and reflector. The coefficient DVR lemma makes $R$ a principal ideal domain, hence Noetherian because each ideal has one generator.

proof.text:
Check the domain for Yoneda first at $\Lambda=A_{E,n}$. Write
$$A_{M,N}=Rf_*H(M,f^!N),\qquad B_{M,N}=H(Rf_!M,N).$$
The unconditional constructible adjunction [lem-sf-constructible-exceptional-adjunction-coefficients] preserves the finite-Tor subcategories, so $f^!N$ and $Rf_!M$ lie there. The dimension-finiteness lemma supplies nonnegative integer bounds $d_X,d_Y$ for $X,Y$ (take zero for an empty scheme). To apply finite constructible internal-Hom preservation without assuming that either scheme is separated over $k$, argue as follows for $W=X,Y$. The finite-type definition gives a finite affine cover $W=\bigcup_{i=1}^tU_i$ by spectra of finitely generated $k$-algebras; these are Noetherian by the affine Noetherian lemma. Restriction to a slice is exact and the derived tensor-pullback comparison commutes with tensor, so restriction preserves the same Tor intervals directly from their definition: a module sheaf $F$ on $U_i$ in degree zero is the restriction of its extension by zero $j_{i,!}F$, so $(K\otimes^L j_{i,!}F)|_{U_i}\cong K|_{U_i}\otimes^L F$. A finite union of the Noetherian affine opens is Noetherian: a descending chain of closed subsets stabilizes on each chart and hence globally after the maximum of the finitely many stabilization indices. Thus the opens and their finite differences used below are constructible. Each $U_i$ is separated over $k$. Apply the internal-Hom corollary on $U_i$, with the single bound $d_W$ (open-subspace dimension monotonicity gives $\dim U_i\le d_W$), and identify its output with the restriction of $H$ by the ringed-site internal-Hom restriction statement. The resulting Tor interval $[c-b-2d_W,e-a+2d_W]$ is independent of $i$. It holds globally: restriction is exact and commutes with tensor, and a cohomology sheaf vanishing on all $U_i$ vanishes. Constructibility also assembles explicitly: intersect each finite local stratification with $U_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}U_j$. These form a finite disjoint locally closed constructible stratification of $W$, with the same locally constant finite restrictions; the common Tor interval bounds the nonzero cohomology degrees. Thus the definitions give bounded constructible finite-Tor internal Homs globally. Apply this argument to $(M,f^!N)$ on $X$ and $(Rf_!M,N)$ on $Y$, and apply the pro-etale direct-image theorem to the first internal Hom. Both $A_{M,N}$ and $B_{M,N}$ therefore lie in the same full category $D^b_{ctf}(Y,A_{E,n})$. For an empty cover the objects are zero. No properness or site-perfectness hypothesis is used.

proof.text: For $\Lambda=R=\mathcal O_E$, the unconditional constructible adjunction puts $f^!N$ and $Rf_!M$ in $D^b_{ctf}$. For each of the two pairs $(M,f^!N)$ on $X$ and $(Rf_!M,N)$ on $Y$, restrict to a finite affine cover of the relevant scheme $W$. On an affine chart use the integral internal-Hom corollary and the finite-level uniform bounds of step 3; restriction of internal Hom is its ringed-site restriction comparison. Choose one dimension bound $d_W$ for all charts. The common finite-reduction Tor interval from that corollary bounds the nonzero cohomology on every chart. Global constructibility is obtained by the finite disjoint refinement $U_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}U_j$ as in step 3. Internal Hom into a derived-complete object is derived complete, and its integral reduction is the evaluation-defined comparison of the integral Hom-reduction lemma. Thus both internal Homs meet the integral definition globally, also when $W$ is not separated. Apply integral direct-image constructibility to $H=H(M,f^!N)$; its statement gives completeness, finite-reduction comparisons and a bound independent of $n$. Finally the residue-Tor theorem identifies $D^b_c(Y,R)$ with $D^b_{ctf}(Y,R)$. Consequently both $A_{M,N}$ and $B_{M,N}$ belong to the same full category used for Yoneda. This argument keeps completed coefficient sheaves distinct from constant integral or condensed coefficients.

proof.text:
Let $\Lambda$ now be finite or integral and $L\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$. Using the adjunctions from steps 1–2, the projection isomorphism, and the ordinary adjunction and the unconditional constructible exceptional adjunction, form the natural bijection $h_L$:
$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(L,B_{M,N})
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!M\otimes^L L,N)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!(M\otimes^L Lf^*L),N)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(M\otimes^L Lf^*L,f^!N)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(Lf^*L,H(M,f^!N))\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(L,A_{M,N}).
\end{aligned}$$
At the integral stage every tensor in this chain is completed tensor. For the second arrow precompose with $\operatorname{PF}_{f,M,L}^{-1}$: its direction is from $Rf_!(M\otimes^LLf^*L)$ to $Rf_!M\otimes^LL$. The projection theorem needs $M$ bounded constructible and $L$ finite-Tor, both available. All intermediate inputs to the exceptional adjunction are finite-Tor and bounded constructible: the finite-Tor pullback lemma applies to $L$ and gives bounded constructibility of $Lf^*L$, tensor with the finite-Tor $M$ preserves it, and integral pullback and completed tensor preserve it by their integral preservation theorem. At integral coefficients the residue-Tor theorem upgrades the constructible outputs to the uniform finite-Tor domain. Hence the constructible exceptional adjunction applies here. For the exceptional arrow use the new constructible-adjunction lemma, which has exactly these coefficient categories and requires no ambient-adjoint datum. The last arrow is the ordinary pullback–direct-image adjunction on bounded constructible objects. These checks justify every bijection without invoking the preservation summary that depends back on this item.

proof.text: The projection isomorphism used above is the actual coefficient-stage projection map: at $A_{E,n}$ it is the finite etale theorem, transported to pro-etale realizations by the pro-etale projection theorem; at $R$ it is the compatible normalized-system isomorphism of the adic theorem; at $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ it is the rational/common-stage projection theorem. The all-stage projection-formula interface identifies these maps and records their coefficient compatibilities. Thus the second bijection uses the inverse of the map with direction $Rf_!M\otimes^LL\to Rf_!(M\otimes^LLf^*L)$, with both $M,L$ finite-Tor; it never applies a projection theorem to an arbitrary bounded-below test object.

proof.text:
Apply the fully faithful Yoneda embedding to the full category $\mathcal C=D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$, which contains both objects by steps 3–4. The natural bijections $h_L$ identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(-,B_{M,N})$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(-,A_{M,N})$. Explicitly set
$$a=h_{B_{M,N}}(1_{B_{M,N}}):B_{M,N}\to A_{M,N},\qquad
b=h_{A_{M,N}}^{-1}(1_{A_{M,N}}):A_{M,N}\to B_{M,N}.$$
Naturality in $L$ says $h_L(u)=a\circ u$ and $h_L^{-1}(v)=b\circ v$. Thus $ab=1_A$ and $ba=1_B$. The required canonical isomorphism has forward map $b$. Naturality of the five bijections in $M$ (contravariantly) and $N$ (covariantly) implies naturality of this isomorphism by the uniqueness part of Yoneda. In particular no extension-by-zero generator theorem, geometric-stalk detection, or unproved equivalence of whole sites is needed.

proof.text:
Check coefficient compatibility for the specified forward map $b:A\to B$ by transposition. Its action on a test map $u:L\to A$ is: transpose by $Lf^*\dashv Rf_*$; transpose tensor--Hom to a map $M\otimes^LLf^*L\to f^!N$; transpose by the constructible exceptional adjunction; precompose with $\operatorname{PF}_{f,M,L}$; transpose tensor--Hom again. For a coefficient functor $T$, insert the canonical comparisons at these five places. The operation-reduction statement identifies tensor, ordinary unit/counit and compact-support comparisons. The unconditional constructible-adjunction lemma gives the explicit unit/counit equations for the exceptional comparison. The projection-formula theorem gives its coefficient square. Internal-Hom comparisons are the transposes of coefficient change of evaluation; they therefore identify the two tensor--Hom transpositions, by their defining universal property. Thus the two composites from $T(A)$ to the new $B$ have the same tensor/evaluation/counit transpose and are equal. This is a global transposition calculation, not an inference that equality of derived maps can be checked on an open cover.

For finite quotients, invertibility of the internal-Hom comparison on an arbitrary finite-type scheme follows by restricting its evaluation-defined map to a finite affine cover and applying the finite-Tor Hom coefficient theorem there; restriction of internal Hom commutes with this construction. A cone is zero if its cohomology sheaves vanish on the cover. This use of locality proves invertibility only. Use the finite direct-image coefficient comparison for $Rf_*$; its pro-etale clause applies because the input has etale origin by the constructible-origin theorem, and the etale witness has the same finite Tor interval by the converse clause (ii) of the comparison Tor-amplitude lemma, as the etale hypothesis of that theorem requires. Integral reduction uses the arbitrary-first-variable integral Hom-reduction comparison, and integral direct image uses its finite-reduction theorem. Finite scalar extension of integral Hom uses its scalar-extension theorem. Hence every comparison invoked is invertible on the stated domains, and the calculation above proves the actual finite-reduction and scalar-extension squares. For field coefficients reduction is always understood on an integral representative before localization. For the ordinary direct-image scalar comparison at a finite extension $E\subset L$, the completed coefficient comparison makes the extended coefficient sheaf finite free of rank $[L:E]$ and identifies integral scalar extension with ordinary tensor by that sheaf. Choose a basis. Tensor then becomes a finite direct sum; additive direct image, its derived functor and the strict-tower limit commute with this finite direct sum. Thus the canonical scalar map is an isomorphism. Its transpose is extension of the old counit, so the same five-arrow transposition calculation applies, independently of the chosen basis.

At a finite coefficient stage scalar extension is also explicit. For a finite extension $E\subset E'$ put $A=A_n$ and $B=\mathcal O_{E'}/\varpi^n\mathcal O_{E'}$; the coefficient-system adjoint statement records that $B$ is finite free over $A$. On each small ringed site choose a K-flat $P$ with flat terms representing $K$, a K-injective $I$ representing $L$, and a B-K-injective resolution $I\otimes_A B\to J$ of $L\otimes_A^L B$. Extension by B is exact, since a choice of A-basis makes its underlying A-module functor a finite direct sum. On sheaves it is left adjoint to restriction: a B-linear map $B\otimes_A F\to G$ is sent to $x\mapsto u(1\otimes x)$, with inverse $b\otimes x\mapsto b v(x)$; the balancing relations and restriction maps give the adjunction directly. The right-adjoint K-injective lemma therefore makes $\operatorname{Res}J$ A-K-injective. The underlying A-complex $I\otimes_A B$ is a finite sum of I and hence A-K-injective, because its Hom complex from an acyclic complex is a finite sum of acyclic Hom complexes. Both represent $L\otimes_A B$; the K-injective derived-Hom identification compares them by a homotopy equivalence. The derived tensor-pullback theorem makes $P\otimes_A B$ K-flat. Consequently the representing internal-Hom complexes give, after restriction to A,
$$\mathcal Hom_B^\bullet(P\otimes_A B,J)=\mathcal Hom_A^\bullet(P,\operatorname{Res}J)\simeq\mathcal Hom_A^\bullet(P,I\otimes_A B)\cong\mathcal Hom_A^\bullet(P,I)\otimes_A B.$$
The first equality is again evaluation on $1\otimes p$ and its inverse $b\otimes p\mapsto b h(p)$. The last isomorphism uses a finite A-basis of B; finite sums commute with every product in the Hom complex, even for unbounded P. The K-flat/K-injective Hom theorem and the internal-Hom construction justify these representatives. The resulting map is the evaluation-defined scalar comparison, so is canonical and intertwines the transpositions above. Restriction of scalars reflects acyclicity, since it leaves the underlying sheaf complex unchanged, giving the required B-linear isomorphism. The finite direct-image coefficient theorem applies to this finite A-algebra B as written. A further quotient reduces to the finite-quotient case already checked, over $E'$, and the coefficient cocycles of the new exceptional-adjunction prerequisite identify the composite comparisons.

proof.text:
The shift compatibility is checked on the same Hom bijection. Under the canonical shift identifications, for any integer $r$,
$$\operatorname{Hom}(L,A_{M,N[r]})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L[-r],A_{M,N}),\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}(L,B_{M,N[r]})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L[-r],B_{M,N}).$$
The five arrows for $(L,N[r])$ identify with those for $(L[-r],N)$: a tensor factor shifted by $r$ shifts the tensor by $r$, and each exact right adjoint's shift comparison is the transpose of the corresponding comparison for its left adjoint. The tensor–Hom comparisons have the signs of the shifted Hom complex; shifting its first variable gives $H(M[r],Q)=H(M,Q)[-r]$, while shifting its second gives $H(M,Q[r])=H(M,Q)[r]$. Both transposition routes therefore use the same signed evaluation map. In the projection definition, the proper projection map is the transpose of $(\varepsilon_p\otimes1)\circ\mu_p$, and the compact-support map is its composite with $Rp_*(\gamma)$, where $\gamma$ is the extension-by-zero tensor comparison followed by pullback composition. Shifting either tensor factor shifts each of these composites by the total-tensor convention, using $d_{C[r]}=(-1)^rd_C$; the evaluation comparison uses that same convention. The shifted composite is therefore the specified shifted projection transformation. Thus $h$ for the shifted arguments is the shifted $h$. By uniqueness in step 7 this proves the shift square for the exchange, in the second variable and, with the negative shift, in the first. Completion commutes with these identifications since its Koszul-limit construction is exact and the completion unit is natural.

proof.text: Pass to the two field stages using their actual definitions. Rationalization keeps the integral objects and replaces each Hom group by its tensor product with $E$. Send the inverse pair $(a,b)$ of step 7 to its images there; their composites remain identities. The integral tensor–Hom bijection and its naturality localize, and the prescribed operations on objects and morphisms are the ones of the datum, so this gives the displayed exchange over $E$. For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, represent the finitely many input objects and maps over a common finite extension $E$. Define the exchange by its $E$-stage map. Step 8 identifies this representative after any larger finite extension, so its class is independent of the representative. The inverse is represented by the inverse at that same stage; naturality and the coefficient and shift equations hold over a common stage and therefore in the directed colimit of Hom groups. This supplies every coefficient stage in the statement without using a theorem on integral or field exceptional adjoints that depends back on this item.

split_report.summary: Expanded the adjunction chain into ten steps, proved the tensor-Hom bijections from ringed-site results, restricted Yoneda tests to the full finite-Tor category containing both outputs, and verified coefficients and shifts by transposition. Added one statement-only prerequisite for the unconditional constructible exceptional adjunction and its coefficient comparisons on general finite-type schemes; the conditional ambient adjunction and the condensed-module variant are not substituted. Statement unchanged.
split_report.blueprint: The unit has one proof paragraph. Steps 1-6 justify and type all five Hom bijections; step 7 gives the inverse Yoneda maps; steps 8-10 verify coefficients, shifts and field/common-stage passage. The source error is the use of all bounded-below etale-origin tests despite the finite-Tor projection hypothesis, repaired by restricting tests after establishing closure.
